meta.title: Why there are two high tides a day, not one

style: .t-page{display:grid;grid-template-rows:auto 1fr auto auto;gap:26px}.t-head h1{font-family:var(--ig-display);font-weight:var(--ig-display-weight);font-size:38px;line-height:1.06;letter-spacing:var(--ig-display-tracking);margin:0 0 10px}.t-head p{margin:0;font-size:15px;color:var(--ig-secondary);max-width:44em}.t-stage{position:relative;display:flex;align-items:center;border-radius:var(--ig-radius);padding:18px 0;background:color-mix(in srgb, var(--ig-accent) 5%, transparent)}.t-stage svg{display:block;width:100%;height:auto;overflow:visible}.t-cols{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1fr 1fr;gap:22px}.t-card{border:1px solid var(--ig-hairline);border-radius:var(--ig-radius);padding:14px 16px}.t-card h2{margin:0 0 6px;font-size:13px;font-weight:700;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;color:var(--ig-accent-text)}.t-card p{margin:0;font-size:14px;line-height:1.45;color:var(--ig-secondary)}.t-card em{font-style:normal;color:var(--ig-ink);font-weight:600}.t-foot{font-size:11.5px;color:var(--ig-muted);border-top:1px solid var(--ig-hairline);padding-top:8px}
body:
Why there are two high tides a day,
and not one

The Moon does not lift one bulge of water. It stretches the whole ocean along one line, and the Earth turns through both ends of it.

The near side

Water closest to the Moon is pulled hardest, so it runs ahead of the solid Earth and piles up.

The far side

Water on the opposite face is pulled least, so the Earth is drawn out from under it and it piles up there too.

A point on the equator passes through both bulges in one rotation, which is why high water arrives roughly every twelve and a half hours rather than every twenty-five.
